/resources/antony-and-cleopatra/themes-c.use: Set the guide’s account of Rome and Egypt beside the scenes themselves, and compare Enobarbus’s description of Cleopatra’s barge with the passage in North’s Plutarch that Shakespeare put into verse.

readings.label: Rome and Egypt
readings.title: The opposition keeps changing
readings.copy: Roman characters call Egypt excessive and undisciplined, yet Rome is also theatrical, competitive and ruthless. The contrast tells us as much about the speaker as it does about either place.

readings.label: Source and stage
readings.title: History becomes performance
readings.copy: Shakespeare draws heavily on North’s Plutarch but gives public history an unstable theatrical life. Messengers, reports and ceremonies compete to determine what the audience believes.

readings.label: The final acts
readings.title: Defeat does not settle meaning
readings.copy: Caesar wins the political contest, but Cleopatra contests his control of the story. Her death leaves open whether a victory in war can ever control how people remember and imagine her.

/resources/shakespeare/gender-power-omka.use: Watch the films beside the plays and follow the guide’s comparisons, from Emilia to Indu and from Lady Macbeth to Nimmi, down to the cummerbund that stands in for the handkerchief.

readings.label: Omkara
readings.title: Evidence enters another culture
readings.copy: The handkerchief becomes a jewelled cummerbund, carrying ideas of marriage, possession and sexual suspicion into a different material and social world.

readings.label: Maqbool
readings.title: Desire is politically dangerous
readings.copy: Nimmi is not a copy of Lady Macbeth. She is Abbaji’s mistress, in a crime family where love and command are the same thing, and that gives her power and puts her in danger.

readings.label: Film form
readings.title: The camera redistributes knowledge
readings.copy: Close-ups, cuts, music and landscape decide what the audience can read in a face or body. Those choices can give women a presence that spoken dialogue alone does not measure.

/resources/macbeth/quick-guide/.use: Write down each prophecy in the witches’ exact words, then follow the guide through Macbeth’s readings of them, from the opening scene to the second prophecies.

readings.label: The witches
readings.title: A greeting is not an instruction
readings.copy: The sisters name possible futures, and Macbeth hears one of them as an order. The space between prophecy and action is where responsibility remains.

readings.label: After Duncan
readings.title: Power cannot finish the crime
readings.copy: The crown does not end Macbeth’s fear. Blood, sleeplessness and the return of the dead show that holding power brings new dangers and does not end the old ones.

readings.label: Equivocation
readings.title: Words become traps
readings.copy: The later apparitions tell truths in forms designed to mislead. Macbeth hears guarantees because he has learned to choose the meaning that best protects his confidence.

/resources/richard-ii/study-guide/.use: Compare the play’s Richard with the historical king, and read the deposition scene with the guide’s account of the performance paid for on the eve of the Essex rising in 1601.

readings.label: Richard
readings.title: Language becomes a kingdom
readings.copy: As Richard loses practical command, his verbal power grows more elaborate. His self-dramatisation can reveal suffering while also showing why performance alone cannot recover political control.

readings.label: Bolingbroke
readings.title: Action looks like necessity
readings.copy: Bolingbroke presents each advance as a limited response to injustice. The accumulation of those apparently practical steps makes a revolution without requiring him to name it at the beginning.

readings.label: Elizabethan stage
readings.title: Deposition was a live danger
readings.copy: Questions of succession and the association with Essex made the play politically charged. Context sharpens the performance without reducing it to a coded report of one event.

/resources/winters-tale/complete-study-g.use: Read the play beside the guide’s account of Greene’s Pandosto, and note the largest change: in Greene the queen dies, and Shakespeare brings Hermione back.

readings.label: Sicilia
readings.title: Jealousy becomes government
readings.copy: Leontes converts a private certainty into public law. Because the accusation comes from a king, misreading damages a marriage, a court, a child and the future of the state.

readings.label: Bohemia
readings.title: Another kind of play begins
readings.copy: In the countryside there is room for youth, music, disguise and comedy. But class and fathers still have power there, so the change of tone is an experiment, and Bohemia is no escape.

readings.label: The statue
readings.title: Wonder does not cancel loss
readings.copy: The final scene offers restoration while keeping its mechanism uncertain. Hermione can return; Mamillius cannot. Reconciliation matters because the play preserves that difference.

/resources/macbeth/summary-analysis/.use: Use the plot and character slides to check your memory of the play, then go back to the scene behind each quotation before you use it in an essay.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Macbeth
readings.copy: Works through what happens in the play and the characters who drive it, then builds towards analysis of theme, Jacobean context and key quotations.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Macbeth thinks aloud, so the soliloquies of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth are the play’s richest evidence. Set them beside the witches’ equivocal prophecies and the recurring language of blood, sleep and darkness.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How far is Macbeth the author of his own destruction?
readings.copy: An answer would weigh his soliloquies before and after Duncan’s murder against the promptings of the witches and Lady Macbeth.

/resources/romeo-and-juliet/summary-guid.use: Use the summary to fix the few days of the action in order, then go back to the scenes the quotations come from.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Romeo and Juliet
readings.copy: The guide retraces the play’s action and characters, ties its themes to the world Shakespeare wrote for, and marks the quotations most worth committing to memory.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: The play’s evidence is dramatic. Note who is on stage and who overhears, how public brawls answer private vows, and how the Prologue announces the ending before the lovers have met.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does Shakespeare make the ending of Romeo and Juliet feel inevitable when the Prologue has already given it away?
readings.copy: An answer would set the Prologue’s promise against particular scenes of choice and accident, cited by act and scene.

/resources/king-lear/summary-guide/.use: Mark the places where the two plots meet, above all the scene near Dover where the blinded Gloucester recognises the mad Lear.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: King Lear
readings.copy: Eighteen slides that hold the Lear and Gloucester plots side by side, following the play through surrendered power, divided families, madness and the slow, costly recovery of sight.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: In a play the evidence is speech under pressure: identify who speaks each line, to whom, and at what point in the action. Track the recurring language of sight and blindness, and set parallel moments from the Lear and Gloucester plots against one another.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: What does the Gloucester plot add to the tragedy of Lear?
readings.copy: An answer should pair precise references from both plots, showing where the parallels hold and where they pointedly diverge.

/resources/shakespeare/tragedies-overvie.use: Test the guide’s pattern on one tragedy you know well, then find the scene where that play breaks it.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Shakespeare
readings.copy: The guide reads the tragedies side by side, from Titus Andronicus to King Lear, asking what their protagonists, plots and preoccupations share, and where each play breaks the pattern.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Comparative claims need evidence from more than one play. Test each recurring structure or character type the guide names against at least two tragedies, and note where the pattern holds and where it strains.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: What, if anything, do Shakespeare’s tragic protagonists have in common?
readings.copy: Support the answer by comparing at least two plays directly, citing scenes in which their protagonists face the same kind of choice.

/resources/midsummer-nights-dream/study-.use: Choose a scene where two plots collide, such as Titania waking to Bottom in his ass’s head, and ask what each group of characters takes the moment to mean.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Midsummer
readings.copy: Follows the lovers, the mechanicals and the fairies into the wood and out again, asking what the play makes of love, dreaming and transformation. There is also material on staging, later adaptations and the epilogue Puck speaks straight to the audience.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: The play marks its speakers by form (the lovers rhyme, the fairies sing, the mechanicals talk prose), so a change of verse is evidence in itself. The rehearsals of Pyramus and Thisbe and Puck’s closing address repay close quotation.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Is love in A Midsummer Night’s Dream ever more than enchantment?
readings.copy: Support an answer with the lovers’ quarrels, the working of the love-juice and the marriages the final act expects us to accept.

/resources/poetry/linton-kwesi-johnson-p.use: Listen to Johnson’s recordings of “Sonny’s Lettah” and “Inglan is a Bitch” before reading the guide, so that the rhythm and the Creole spelling reach you as sound.

readings.label: Language
readings.title: Writing in Creole
readings.copy: Johnson’s spelling and grammar are not departures from an imagined neutral English. They carry history, sound and authority, asking the reader to meet the poem on its own linguistic ground.

readings.label: Performance
readings.title: Rhythm gathers an audience
readings.copy: The printed line is one part of the work. Repetition, pace and dub performance make one person’s testimony into something a crowd can hear and answer.

readings.label: Policing
readings.title: Power enters ordinary space
readings.copy: Streets, homes and workplaces become political through surveillance and confrontation. The poems show what the institution does to people day by day: where they can go, whether they are safe, whether they belong.

/resources/pamela/psychological-analysis.use: Date the letters as you read and follow Pamela’s fear and resistance from one to the next, including the delay before she finally leaves.

readings.label: Epistolary form
readings.title: Feeling has no safe distance
readings.copy: Letters place the reader close to uncertainty. Pamela repeats herself, revises a judgement and records danger before she can know how an episode will end.

readings.label: Reception
readings.title: Pamelists and Antipamelists
readings.copy: In the 1740s readers divided over whether Pamela was sincere or calculating, and over what her marriage meant for the order of rank. Fielding’s Shamela (1741) took the calculating view.

readings.label: Power
readings.title: Contradiction needs context
readings.copy: Pamela’s feelings cannot be separated from dependence, confinement and unequal authority. A psychological reading becomes stronger when it measures the conditions under which a choice is made.

/resources/regency/pride-prejudice-key-q.use: Learn each quotation with its speaker and its chapter, and check the guide’s reading of it against the scene before you use it in an essay.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Pride and Prejudice
readings.copy: The guide gathers the quotations most worth carrying into an essay on Austen’s novel, each with a brief note tying it to character, courtship, class or the workings of judgement.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Check the exact exchange or paragraph. Austen often creates judgement through narrative distance, timing and differences between speech and narration.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does Austen use the gap between speech and narration to direct our judgement of her characters?
readings.copy: Support the answer with exact quotations, noting in each case who speaks, who listens and how the narration frames the exchange.

/resources/dorian-gray/introduction/.use: Use the guide to follow influence at work: Wotton’s talk, the yellow book and the changing portrait each record what acting on a theory costs.

readings.label: Influence
readings.title: Language acts upon a life
readings.copy: Lord Henry’s conversation gives Dorian ways to imagine youth, pleasure and loss. Does Lord Henry’s influence excuse what Dorian does, or does it make his responsibility harder to pin down?

readings.label: Art and secrecy
readings.title: The surface does not stay innocent
readings.copy: Basil’s portrait begins as art and becomes evidence. Its changing body records the history that Dorian’s unchanged face allows society to ignore.

readings.label: Oscar Wilde
readings.title: Biography matters, and has limits
readings.copy: The novel’s revisions, reception and Wilde’s later trials belong to its history. They add to the context without making every character or desire into a coded fact about Wilde.

/resources/frankenstein/study-guide/.use: Use the guide to keep the three narrators distinct. Walton’s letters hold Victor’s account, which holds the creature’s, and each telling asks to be judged as well as heard.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Frankenstein
readings.copy: Twenty-two slides that work inward through the novel’s frames, from Walton’s letters to Victor’s account to the creature’s own story, weighing creation against responsibility and knowledge against isolation.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Walton’s letters enclose Victor’s narrative, which in turn contains the creature’s, so every claim in the novel has a teller with an interest in it. Quote the competing narrators on the same events and weigh their versions against one another.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Who bears the greater responsibility for the creature’s crimes: Victor, or the society that rejects his creation?
readings.copy: An answer needs quotations from the creature’s own narrative as well as Victor’s, set against what each account is trying to excuse.

/resources/great-expectations/study-guid.use: Use the guide to keep the two Pips apart: the boy who acts and the narrator who judges him, often in the same sentence.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Great Expectations
readings.copy: Twenty-one slides following Pip from the forge to London and back, watching class, crime, memory and generosity entangle until the novel arrives at its own idea of what a gentleman is.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: The story is told by an older Pip judging his younger self, so the narration itself is evidence: notice where hindsight, shame or irony colours the telling. Scenes with Joe, Magwitch and Miss Havisham give the sharpest material on class, crime and generosity.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does the older Pip’s narration judge the expectations of his younger self?
readings.copy: Support an answer with passages in which the narrating Pip comments on, mocks or mourns his earlier conduct, with exact references.

/resources/dracula/complete-overview/.use: Use the guide to track the novel’s paper trail. Letters, diaries, phonograph records and newspaper cuttings build the case against the Count, and no narrator holds it all.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Dracula
readings.copy: Eighteen slides covering the whole novel: the shape of the plot from Transylvania to London and back, the principal characters, the Victorian contexts, and the diaries, letters and cuttings from which the case against the Count is built.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: The novel is assembled from journals, letters, a phonograph diary, a ship’s log and newspaper cuttings, so every quotation has a named writer with partial knowledge. Note who records each event, what that writer cannot yet know, and how the collated papers become the hunters’ weapon.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Why does Stoker tell the story through a collection of documents, with no single narrator?
readings.copy: An answer should cite particular diary entries, letters and cuttings, showing what the fragmented record achieves that one voice could not.

/resources/dracula/gender-roles/.use: Use the guide to see how the novel handles Victorian ideas of conduct: Lucy’s three suitors, Mina’s secretarial work and the jokes about the New Woman all carry its argument about gender.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Dracula
readings.copy: Sixteen slides on what the novel does with men and women: Lucy and Mina compared, the figure of the New Woman, and the anxieties about desire, conduct and masculinity that the vampire drags into the open.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Compare how the novel’s documents describe Lucy and Mina before and after the Count reaches them. Mina’s own journal, Lucy’s letters and the men’s protective language give exact evidence for how female conduct is praised, policed and punished.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does Stoker use Lucy and Mina to show late-Victorian worries about the New Woman?
readings.copy: Support an answer with the documents each woman writes and the language the men use about her, noting how both change as the novel proceeds.

/resources/victorian/a-charles-dickens-c.use: Use the guide to set the Christmas books beside the season they helped remake, from the charity arguments of 1843 to the family rituals the stories assume.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Charles Dickens
readings.copy: The guide follows Dickens’s part in remaking the English Christmas, showing how A Christmas Carol and the Christmas books that followed it bound the season to charity, family and the fireside.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the books and the customs
readings.copy: The evidence here is partly literary and partly social. Test the guide’s claims against the Christmas books themselves, beginning with A Christmas Carol, and against what Victorians recorded of their own festivities in letters, periodicals and the illustrated papers.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How far was the Victorian Christmas Dickens’s invention?
readings.copy: An answer would set scenes from A Christmas Carol and the later Christmas books against customs the Victorians already kept, citing both.

/resources/victorian/ghost-stories-in-li.use: Use the guide to weigh each story as testimony. Note who tells it, what the teller claims to have seen, and what its first audiences were prepared to believe.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Ghost stories
readings.copy: The guide treats the ghost story as evidence of the living: what a culture’s tales of the dead show about its beliefs, its memories and its fears, from fireside telling to the Victorian ghost story at its height.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the tales and their tellers
readings.copy: The evidence lies in the tales and their tellers. Note who narrates each story, what the teller claims to have seen, and what its first audiences were prepared to believe; then set the literary ghost story beside the folk belief it draws on.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Do ghost stories depend on their audiences believing in ghosts?
readings.copy: An answer would draw on particular tales, their narrators and their occasions, alongside what is known of the beliefs of those who first told and heard them.

/resources/victorian/christmas-tradition.use: Use the guide to date each custom. Trees, cards, carols and crackers all entered Christmas at particular moments, and the illustrated papers record their spread.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Victorian Christmas
readings.copy: The guide traces how the Victorians assembled the Christmas we still keep, from the tree, the card and the carol revival to the family dinner and the season’s reading.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the dated evidence
readings.copy: A history of customs rests on dated evidence: early Christmas cards, carol collections, the seasonal numbers of the illustrated papers, and Victorians’ own recollections of how the day was kept.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Which parts of the modern Christmas really are Victorian inventions?
readings.copy: Support the answer with dated evidence, such as an early card, a carol book or a magazine’s Christmas number.

/resources/victorian/how-literature-shap.use: Use the guide to follow the borrowings: which monsters, revenants and rituals Halloween took from fiction, and which customs the fiction took from older observance.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Halloween
readings.copy: The guide follows Halloween from Celtic ritual to the present, showing how ghost stories and the great Gothic novels supplied the festival with its imagery of monsters, hauntings and the dark.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the festival’s sources
readings.copy: A festival’s history is read in mixed evidence: the Gothic novels whose monsters Halloween borrowed, the ghost stories told in season, and the songs, periodicals and recollections that record how the night was actually kept.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How much of the modern Halloween did literature invent?
readings.copy: An answer would pair a custom or image of the festival with its literary source and show when and how the borrowing happened.

/resources/modern/kite-runner-walkthroug.use: Use the walkthrough a section at a time, and keep asking how far Amir, telling the story as an adult, judges the boy he was.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Kite Runner
readings.copy: Walks through Hosseini’s novel from Amir’s childhood in Kabul through exile in America to his return. The commentary comes back again and again to betrayal, guilt and what it really takes to make amends.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Amir narrates as an adult confessing his childhood, so notice where his account slows down and where it looks away. The novel also argues through repetition: kites, scars and echoed phrases return carrying new weight.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Does The Kite Runner allow Amir a genuine atonement for his betrayal of Hassan?
readings.copy: Trace the guilt from the alley in Kabul to the rescue of Sohrab, and weigh what the ending resolves against what it leaves open.

/resources/modern/handmaids-tale-guide/.use: Note each word Gilead coins or takes from scripture, and use the guide to separate what Offred tells you from what she says she cannot.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Handmaid’s Tale
readings.copy: Takes Gilead apart as a system: who holds power, how language, religion and ritual enforce it, and where memory and resistance persist. Offred’s way of telling her story is treated as a subject in its own right.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Offred admits she is reconstructing events, so her hesitations and second versions are evidence too. So are Gilead’s coined names and official phrases, and the Historical Notes that reframe the whole account.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does Gilead use language to control women in The Handmaid’s Tale?
readings.copy: Support the answer with the regime’s renamings, set phrases and ban on reading, and with the moments where Offred plays with words in private.

/resources/modern/half-of-a-yellow-sun-d.use: Note at the start of each chapter whose point of view it takes and which part of the decade it is in, since the novel moves back and forth between the early and the late sixties.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Half of a Yellow Sun
readings.copy: Sets Adichie’s novel against the Biafran war, and compares how the conflict looked from inside Nigeria and from abroad. Richard, Olanna and Ugwu are read as partial witnesses, each seeing and missing different things.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: The evidence lies in the novel’s rotating points of view and its movement between the early and late sixties. Compare how Richard, Olanna and Ugwu register the same war, and notice who finally writes the book within the book.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Who earns the right to tell Biafra’s story in Half of a Yellow Sun?
readings.copy: An answer would set Richard’s abandoned book against Ugwu’s writing, citing what each character witnesses and what each fails to see.

/resources/modern/wide-sargasso-sea-a-st.use: Note who narrates each part (Antoinette, then mostly her husband, then Antoinette in the attic at Thornfield) and where the novel sends you back to Jane Eyre.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Wide Sargasso Sea
readings.copy: An orientation to Rhys’s novel: how the three parts fit together, who narrates each and where they are set, from the Caribbean estates to an attic in England. The book’s central concerns are drawn out along the way.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: The telling is divided between Antoinette and the husband who is never named, so every claim should say whose account it rests on. Dreams, renamings and the novel’s echoes of Jane Eyre are the other places to look for evidence.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does the divided narration of Wide Sargasso Sea answer the story told in Jane Eyre?
readings.copy: Compare Antoinette’s opening and closing sections with the husband’s central account, citing passages where their versions of events diverge.

/resources/modern/wide-sargasso-sea-post.use: Read the guide with the novel’s history in mind: the Emancipation Act of 1833, and what it changed for Antoinette’s family and the people who had worked for them.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Wide Sargasso Sea
readings.copy: The guide reads Rhys’s novel against the history of empire and emancipation, following how race, language and displacement press on a heroine whose identity is never securely her own. It also looks at who tells the story, and what each telling leaves out.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: The novel’s evidence lies in its divided narration. Set Antoinette’s account beside her husband’s, notice what each omits, and watch how renaming, silence and shifts of language carry meanings neither voice will state outright.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does Rhys use divided narration to contest whose version of Antoinette’s story we believe?
readings.copy: An answer would weigh passages from each narrator against one another, citing moments where naming, language or silence betrays what the speaker cannot admit.

/resources/modern/wide-sargasso-sea-part.use: Mark each point where the narration passes between the husband and Antoinette, and what each of them knows that the other does not.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Wide Sargasso Sea
readings.copy: A close reading of the novel’s long middle section, where the husband takes over the telling. It follows the marriage at Granbois from first unease to open breakdown, and watches narration, rumour and money tilt the balance of power.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Most of this section reaches us through the husband’s voice, briefly interrupted by Antoinette’s, and that handover matters. Daniel Cosway’s letters, the talk of obeah and the renaming of Antoinette as Bertha are the crucial pieces of evidence.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How far is the husband responsible for the collapse of the marriage in Part 2 of Wide Sargasso Sea?
readings.copy: Weigh his narration against what it lets slip: the letters he chooses to believe, the name he imposes and the interlude in which Antoinette speaks.

/resources/modern/wide-sargasso-sea-part.use: Read Part Three with the fire at Thornfield in Jane Eyre in mind, and compare Antoinette’s dream with what Brontë’s novel reports.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Wide Sargasso Sea
readings.copy: A reading of the novel’s brief final section, narrated by Antoinette from the room where she is kept in England. It follows confinement, broken memory and the recurring dream towards the fire, and towards the novel’s meeting with Jane Eyre.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Antoinette narrates from the attic, framed by Grace Poole’s voice, and her confusion about time and place is itself evidence. The third dream, the red dress and the final sentences deserve the closest reading.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Is the ending of Wide Sargasso Sea a defeat or an act of self-assertion?
readings.copy: An answer rests on the wording of Antoinette’s last dream and her final waking words, and on how much the novel allows us to see beyond them.

/resources/american/langston-hughes-chai.use: Read the guide as the history of a document: who gave the testimony, who wrote it down, where Hughes’s foreword was printed, and how it came to be found again.

readings.title: A meeting on the road
readings.copy: Travelling with Zora Neale Hurston, Hughes encountered an escaped chain-gang prisoner. That meeting linked a private act of survival to a much wider history of forced labour in the South.

readings.title: A foreword crosses languages
readings.copy: Writing from Moscow early in 1933, Hughes supplied the foreword to the Soviet edition of John L. Spivak’s 1932 book on the Georgia chain gangs. It appeared only in Russian and was never included in English copies.

readings.title: The archive speaks again
readings.copy: Steven Hoelscher’s research brought the forgotten text back into English. Its recovery shows that literary history depends upon catalogues, correspondence and the patient reconstruction of incomplete records.

/resources/american/langston-hughes-dont.use: Read “Mother to Son” aloud first, then follow the staircase image into King’s speeches and Obama’s, noting what each speaker keeps and what each changes.

readings.label: Langston Hughes
readings.title: The staircase carries a voice
readings.copy: In ‘Mother to Son’ a mother describes her life as a staircase she has kept climbing. The staircase is the famous part, but the poem’s force is also in the way the mother talks straight to her son.

readings.label: Martin Luther King Jr
readings.title: Echo becomes shared language
readings.copy: King repeatedly returned to the poem’s movement and phrasing. The borrowing lets different voices and histories meet within a living tradition of speech.

readings.label: Barack Obama
readings.title: The image travels again
readings.copy: Obama’s 2008 language renews the ascent for another political moment. Following that return reveals how literary influence can survive through memory, rhythm and communal recognition.

/resources/moby-dick/study-guide/.use: Pick one chapter where the book changes form (Father Mapple’s sermon, a scene set out as a play, a chapter of whale science) and ask what Ishmael can say in that form that plain narrative would not let him.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Moby-Dick
readings.copy: Tracks the Pequod’s voyage and its crew, with the history of nineteenth-century whaling behind it. Particular attention goes to Ishmael’s way of telling the story, which changes shape as the book goes on.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Note which form a passage takes before deciding what it shows: Ishmael’s narration, Ahab’s quarter-deck rhetoric, a sermon, a cetology chapter and a scene laid out like a play each offer a different kind of evidence.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Why does Melville give the telling of Moby-Dick to Ishmael, and not to Ahab?
readings.copy: Draw evidence from the opening chapters, from Ishmael’s digressions, and from the scenes where his voice recedes and Ahab’s takes over.

/resources/american/biography-of-harper-.use: Read it beside the novel to separate Monroeville from Maycomb: what Lee took from her childhood town and her friendship with Truman Capote, and what she made up.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: Harper Lee
readings.copy: Follows Harper Lee from her Alabama childhood through the New York years to the literary career crowned by To Kill a Mockingbird. The life and the novel are kept in sight of each other throughout.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the dates and places
readings.copy: A life is evidenced by dates, places and publication records. Where the guide connects Lee’s Alabama upbringing to To Kill a Mockingbird, test the link against the novel itself: its small-town setting and its child narrator.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How far does To Kill a Mockingbird grow out of Harper Lee’s own Alabama childhood?
readings.copy: Set dated biographical detail beside particular scenes, and let the novel’s child narrator complicate any one-to-one reading.

/resources/american/to-kill-a-mockingbir.use: Use the character list to keep Maycomb’s families straight, then test each theme against the trial chapters, where the town shows what it believes.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: To Kill a Mockingbird
readings.copy: A working map of Maycomb across twenty-one slides. The guide sets out the novel’s principal characters and shows how each one carries its arguments about justice, prejudice, childhood and moral courage.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Scout tells the story as an adult remembering her childhood, so notice where the child’s understanding and the adult’s hindsight pull apart. The trial scenes and Atticus’s courtroom speech supply the most exact evidence for questions about justice and prejudice.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does Scout’s childhood perspective shape the novel’s treatment of prejudice?
readings.copy: An answer needs moments where the narration splits between the child who watches and the adult who remembers, tied to precise references to the trial.

/resources/american/turning-point-in-the.use: Read chapter 7 beside the guide and mark the line where the afternoon at the Plaza turns against Gatsby.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Great Gatsby
readings.copy: Nine slides on the scene at the Plaza, where Gatsby loses Daisy just when he seems to have won her back.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: A turning point is proved by close reading. Quote the dialogue of the confrontation itself and Nick’s observation of it, then set passages from before and after the scene side by side to show exactly what has changed.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: At what moment does Gatsby’s dream become unrecoverable, and how does Fitzgerald mark it?
readings.copy: Support an answer with quotations from the scene you identify as the pivot and from the chapters on either side of it.

/resources/american/biography-of-f-scott.use: Use the biography to place the novel: Fitzgerald wrote The Great Gatsby in 1923–24 and published it in 1925, after the Princeton years, the marriage to Zelda and the money troubles the guide describes.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: F. Scott Fitzgerald
readings.copy: A life of Fitzgerald told alongside his books, from Jazz Age celebrity through the shifting fortunes of his reputation. The career becomes a way of reading The Great Gatsby more closely.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the records and dates
readings.copy: A biography argues from records: dates, titles, publication history. Where an episode of Fitzgerald’s life is set beside The Great Gatsby, check that the dates hold and that the novel bears the comparison out.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How did Fitzgerald’s Jazz Age career shape The Great Gatsby, and where does the novel resist a biographical reading?
readings.copy: An answer needs dated events from Fitzgerald’s life placed beside particular passages of the novel.

/resources/american/corruption-the-ameri.use: Take each symbol the guide discusses (the green light, the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, the valley of ashes) back to the passages where it appears, and note who sees it and when.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Great Gatsby
readings.copy: Takes the novel’s recurring symbols one by one: what damaged kind of success each one stands for, and what illusion it protects. Corruption is read through the images.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Fitzgerald gives his evidence as recurring images (the green light, the valley of ashes, the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg) and as the distance between Gatsby’s parties and what pays for them. Follow each symbol through all its appearances.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does Fitzgerald use recurring symbols to expose the corruption beneath the novel’s versions of success?
readings.copy: Quote each symbol at more than one appearance and show what changes between them.

/resources/american/death-of-a-character.use: Follow the deaths in order, Myrtle’s, then Gatsby’s and Wilson’s, and ask which relationships each one exposes and who is left to deal with it.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Great Gatsby
readings.copy: Reads one of the novel’s deaths backwards through the relationships that prepare for it, asking whose loyalty gives way and when. The marriages and affairs matter here as causes.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: The evidence lies in the novel’s pairings (the marriages, the affairs, the loyalties strained between them) and in the scenes where a promise is made or broken. Note who is present at each turning point and what each character chooses there.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Whose failures weigh most in the death at the centre of The Great Gatsby?
readings.copy: Trace the sequence of scenes that leads to the death, citing the choice each character makes along the way.

/resources/american/great-gatsby-essay-p.use: Use the plan as a model, then replace its evidence with quotations you have found yourself, so the essay argues from your own reading of the novel.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Great Gatsby
readings.copy: A worked plan for an essay on setting, symbolism and the American Dream, showing how to move from the novel’s places and images to a sustained argument.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Fitzgerald’s settings are the essay’s raw material: West Egg and East Egg, the valley of ashes between them, and the city beyond. Each place earns its paragraph when it is quoted at the moment it carries symbolic weight.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does Fitzgerald use setting and symbol to question the American Dream in The Great Gatsby?
readings.copy: Build each paragraph around one place or image, supported by a quoted passage and tied back to the argument.

/resources/american/admiration-for-gatsb.use: Read it with the first chapter open, where Nick makes Gatsby the one exception to his scorn, and ask how that early verdict colours everything he tells you afterwards.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Great Gatsby
readings.copy: The guide asks why Nick comes to admire a man he knows to be partly invented. It sets Gatsby’s hope and reinvention against his deceptions, and follows the moral choices that push Nick towards a verdict.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: The novel’s evidence is Nick’s own telling: his opening claim to reserve judgement, the rumours traded at Gatsby’s parties, and the moments where he praises Gatsby outright. Watch where his wording shifts from report to admiration.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How far does Nick’s admiration for Gatsby survive what he learns about him?
readings.copy: Support an answer with Nick’s direct judgements of Gatsby from early and late in the novel, noting what each judgement follows.

/resources/american/things-we-admire-abo.use: Pick one scene for each quality the guide admires and ask whether the admiration is Nick’s or the novel’s.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Great Gatsby
readings.copy: Eleven slides on what is admirable about Gatsby. The guide works through his hope, his loyalty and the imaginative self-creation that set him apart from the world he tries to enter.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Gatsby reaches the reader through Nick Carraway’s retrospective narration, so weigh Nick’s judgements against what Gatsby actually says and does. His parties, his mannered speech and the green light at the end of Daisy’s dock all give precise, quotable evidence.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How far does the novel want us to admire Gatsby, and how far to judge him?
readings.copy: Support an answer with Nick’s explicit verdicts on Gatsby and with the scenes in which his hope and loyalty are put under pressure.

/resources/american/the-great-gatsby-cha.use: For each character, find the scene the guide points to and decide what that person is protecting, remembering that every description reaches you through Nick.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Great Gatsby
readings.copy: A character-by-character reading of the novel that judges each figure by their relationships and by the values their choices expose. The argument rests on what characters decide.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Character in this novel arrives twice over: in what people say and do, and in how Nick chooses to describe them. Set dialogue and action beside Nick’s commentary, and note where the two pull apart.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How does Fitzgerald use the contrast between Gatsby and Tom Buchanan to weigh the values of their world?
readings.copy: Compare scenes in which each man uses his wealth, citing both dialogue and Nick’s commentary on it.

/resources/american/the-great-gatsby-cor.use: Use the guide to keep a ledger: who spends money in the novel, who earns it, and who pays when the summer ends.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Great Gatsby
readings.copy: Treats the novel as an argument about America, in which wealth, carelessness and Gatsby’s self-invention each test the country’s promise from a different side.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Watch where money acts in the novel: the parties, the houses, the casual damage the rich leave behind, and the invented past Gatsby builds his pursuit on. The critique lives in the distance between the dream’s language and the novel’s outcomes.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: Does The Great Gatsby condemn the American Dream itself, or only its corruption?
readings.copy: Separate the passages that honour Gatsby’s hope from those that count what it costs, and quote from both.

/resources/american/the-great-gatsby-not.use: Treat each critical reading in the guide as an argument to test: find the passage it rests on, and decide whether the novel supports it.

readings.label: Guide summary
readings.title: The Great Gatsby
readings.copy: Close-reading notes on the narration, imagery and structure, set beside what critics have made of them. The aim is to test readings at the level of the sentence.

readings.label: Textual evidence
readings.title: Check the language and form
readings.copy: Every claim here can be tested against the page: Nick’s retrospective narration, the recurring images, the ordering of the chapters. Where a critical interpretation is offered, find the passage it depends on before adopting it.

readings.label: Study question
readings.title: How far does Nick’s narration control the reader’s judgement in The Great Gatsby?
readings.copy: Close-read passages where Nick withholds, delays or colours information, and cite critics only where the text supports them.

/resources/american/moby-dick-1851-publi.use: Keep the two first editions apart: what the British text left out, how its reviewers responded, and why the book had to wait for a revival.

/resources/american/puddnhead-wilson-189.use: Watch the arithmetic: Roxy is one-sixteenth Black and her son one thirty-second, enough under the law to make him a slave, which is why she exchanges the two babies.

/resources/american/white-fang-1906/.use: Read it beside The Call of the Wild, whose journey runs the other way, and keep the novel’s animal point of view apart from the arguments of the nature-fakers row.

/resources/ancient-epic/iliad-samuel-but.use: Keep Butler’s choices in view as you read: prose for Homer’s verse, Roman names such as Jove and Minerva for the Greek gods, and the war’s events the poem leaves to other stories.

/resources/modern/blackwood-the-willows/.use: Follow the narrator and the Swede down the Danube with the guide, noting how much the story leaves unexplained and where the landscape itself becomes the threat.

/resources/poetry/ancient-mariner-versio.use: Read a stanza in the 1798 text and the same stanza in the revised poem with its marginal gloss, and ask what the gloss adds.

/resources/poetry/paradise-lost-publicat.use: Use the guide alongside the poem’s front matter: the Arguments, the note on “The Verse” and the change from ten books to twelve.

/resources/poetry/pope-lock-and-criticis.use: Read the dressing-table scene and the game of ombre with the guide, and compare the two-canto Rape of the Lock with the five-canto version that brought in the sylphs.

/resources/renaissance-early-modern/arde.use: Set the play beside Holinshed’s account of the murder of Thomas Arden in 1551, and use the guide to see what the dramatist kept, changed and added.

/resources/renaissance-early-modern/duch.use: Read Act IV, the imprisonment, with the guide’s account of the indoor Blackfriars stage, and ask what a small, candlelit playhouse did for those scenes.

/resources/renaissance-early-modern/sir-.use: Read Hand D’s three pages, the riot scene in which More quiets the crowd, with the guide, and keep the evidence for Shakespeare’s authorship apart from the claims made for it.

/resources/shakespeare/hamlet-three-text.use: Compare “To be, or not to be” as Q1 prints it with the familiar version, and weigh the competing accounts the guide gives of where Q1 came from.

/resources/shakespeare/king-lear-two-tex.use: Keep the 1608 Quarto and the 1623 Folio apart as you read, and note which scenes and lines each has that the other lacks.

/resources/shakespeare/macbeth-folio-and.use: Read the Hecate scenes and the witches’ songs with the guide’s case for Middleton’s hand, and set Simon Forman’s 1611 account of a performance beside the Folio text.

/resources/shakespeare/othello-two-texts.use: Compare a few speeches in the 1622 Quarto and the Folio, and notice the oaths missing from the Folio, removed after the 1606 Act to Restrain Abuses of Players.

/resources/victorian/dracula-1897-origin.use: Read the Whitby chapters and the log of the Demeter with the guide, and keep what Stoker’s working notes show apart from what later writers have claimed about Vlad the Impaler.

/resources/victorian/gogol-overcoat-the-.use: Follow the money with the guide (Akaky’s salary, Petrovitch’s price and the savings the coat takes), then read the ending with the Person of Consequence in mind.

/resources/victorian/moonstone-1868/.use: List the narrators in order as you read, from Betteredge onwards, and use the guide to ask what each is in a position to know.
